dailyBrief.text: Good morning — the warm spell is over: Solon turns partly cloudy and much cooler today, high near 56° after yesterday's 76°, with a chilly low around 38° tonight. Overnight, Iran said four oil tankers hit mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, a day after the U.S. said the main lanes were cleared, and Binance disclosed a $6.3 billion hack, the biggest theft in crypto history. The Cavs rallied late but fell 114-111 at Atlanta — Harden had 24 and Mitchell 22 — and they're back at it Halloween night in Milwaukee. Today locally, early in-person voting runs 7:30 AM to 7:30 PM, Jurassic Quest opens downtown, and Pumpkins & Piranhas has its final night at the aquarium.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
Russian strikes kill at least 19 across Ukraine, including 15 at Dnipro's main station
items.summary:
A Russian drone struck the main railway station in Dnipro on Thursday morning as passengers waited to board, killing 15 people there, according to Ukrainian authorities in the latest count. At least 19 people died across the country that day, including two 15-year-old girls in Chernihiv and three people hit in a residential building in the Poltava region, and Kyiv was struck by ballistic missiles again on Thursday night.

Ukraine's rail operator said a jet-powered drone hit a platform where a commuter train and a passenger train bound for Zaporizhzhia were standing. Images from the scene showed bodies on the platform and rescuers carrying the wounded away, while a separate drone killed an employee of the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant, according to the international atomic energy agency.

The attacks came even as a narrow local ceasefire held in the southern Kherson region, where Russia and Ukraine have paused fighting around occupied Oleshky since Tuesday to let humanitarian aid in. That truce, brokered with involvement from the U.S. first lady's office, is set to run until late on November 1, and some residents were evacuated from Oleshky on Friday.

President Volodymyr Zelensky called the station strike deliberate and cruel and renewed calls for sanctions and more air defence, as Ukrainian officials warn of a shortage of air-defence missiles heading into winter.

items.title: G20 foreign ministers skip their traditional group photo over Russia's presence in Atlanta
items.summary:
Foreign ministers from the G20 began their meeting in Atlanta on Friday without the traditional group photo, after European ministers objected to posing alongside Russia's Sergei Lavrov. The U.S. State Department's agenda for the two-day meeting did not include the family shot at all.

Germany's foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, said plainly that there would be no photo of European partners together with Lavrov, because there is no normalcy in relations with Russia. European officials had floated taking two separate pictures, one with Lavrov and one without, before the photo was dropped entirely.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is hosting under the U.S. rotating presidency, with an agenda built around energy, supply chains, artificial intelligence and countering China's grip on critical minerals. South Africa was not invited, and the EU's foreign policy chief said she would press for more support for Ukraine and for accountability through a special tribunal.

The Atlanta meeting sets up the leaders' summit in Miami on December 14 to 16. Diplomats expect the same rifts over Ukraine and the Middle East to make a unified final statement hard to reach.

items.title: Israel's final election results leave no bloc with a majority, and Arab parties hold the balance
items.summary:
Israel's Central Elections Committee released final results on Friday: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud-led bloc won 53 seats, the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party won 48, and Arab-led parties won a record 19. In a 120-seat Knesset, 61 seats are needed to govern, so no side can form a government alone.

Likud stayed the largest single party with 27 seats, but Netanyahu's outgoing coalition partners had held 68 seats, meaning his bloc shed 15. Turnout reached 77.9 percent, the highest in decades, with more than 5.7 million ballots cast, and a surge in Arab voting helped lift the Joint List and Ra'am into a possible kingmaker role.

Netanyahu and Likud have claimed the vote was stolen through bribery and foreign funding aimed at Arab parties. The elections committee's director general rejected claims of widespread fraud as baseless and said the election was conducted lawfully, and Qatar denied being the foreign power alleged.

Official results go to President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday, November 4, and the new Knesset is sworn in on November 10. Herzog will consult the parties and give one candidate 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, to build a coalition — and failure could mean yet another election, with Netanyahu staying on as caretaker in the meantime.

items.title: Dockworkers strike at 113 ports in 22 countries over arms shipments and seafarers killed in wars
items.summary:
Dockworkers walked out on Friday at 113 ports in 22 countries, disrupting cargo and ferry traffic in a coordinated protest against ports being used to ship weapons and against the rising number of seafarers killed in wars from the Gulf to the Black Sea. More than 25 unions backed the one-day action.

Major hubs including Piraeus, Valencia, Le Havre, Algeciras and Genoa were hit, along with Tangier Med in Morocco and Nhava Sheva in India. In Piraeus about 3,000 dockworkers and seafarers joined, cargo work stalled and ferries to the Greek islands were suspended. Strikers also demanded pay rises, better conditions and doctors aboard ships crossing war zones.

A Greek seafarers' union counted 28 attacks on vessels in the Gulf in the first 21 days of October, a record since the Iran war began, and 570 confirmed attacks in the Black Sea this year, with 40 seafarers dead and hundreds wounded. An activist group said the stoppage would halt some 52,000 containers and about $2.8 billion in cargo, a figure Reuters could not independently verify.

The strike grows out of a declaration signed in Istanbul in May by dockworkers' unions from more than 35 European countries, demanding that ports not be used to move weapons to war zones.

items.title: Russia's last independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, says it will shut down on November 9
items.summary:
Novaya Gazeta, Russia's best-known independent newspaper, announced on Friday that it will close on November 9 after more than three decades. The paper said prosecutors had pursued its senior journalists and that it had been left without money, an office or a way to collect reader donations.

In its statement, the paper said it had been stripped of all its resources, leaving staff homeless, without means of existence and under constant threat of repression, and that Russian authorities and security services had forced it to stop. Its website was already blocked in Russia and its media registration had been cancelled, and in September it was labelled a foreign agent.

The newspaper was formerly led by Dmitry Muratov, who shared the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize, and six of its journalists have been murdered over the years, including investigative reporter Anna Politkovskaya. Pressure on independent media has intensified since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, under laws that impose long prison terms for discrediting the army.

Amnesty International called the closure a devastating loss for independent journalism in Russia. There was no immediate comment from Russian authorities. A separate exile edition, Novaya Gazeta Europe, based in Riga, is a different publication and is not the operation closing.

items.title: China's stealth attack drone makes its first takeoff and landing on its new amphibious assault ship
items.summary:
China's GJ-21 stealth drone has completed its first takeoff and landing aboard the Sichuan, the country's first Type 076 amphibious assault ship, state news agency Xinhua reported on Friday. Beijing called it a breakthrough for the programme, showing that large Chinese naval ships can operate fixed-wing stealth drones.

The Sichuan, launched in December 2024, displaces more than 40,000 tons at full load and carries an electromagnetic catapult, arresting gear, a full-length flight deck and a twin-island superstructure. It can carry drones, helicopters and amphibious equipment, and state television said it ran consecutive sea trials in late October at undisclosed locations.

The GJ-21, first shown at last year's Beijing military parade, is a reconnaissance and strike drone. A Chinese military expert cited by state media said it has a substantial combat radius for its size, costs far less than crewed stealth jets or hypersonic missiles, can be recovered and reused, and can carry small guided bombs.

Reuters framed the trial as part of Beijing's decades-long military modernisation, which is weaving drones into its fleets of advanced warships, fighters and missiles — a shift the U.S. and its allies are watching closely in the Pacific.

items.title: Trump puts his Kansas and Iowa rallies back on, a day after canceling them
items.summary:
President Trump's weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa are back on, a White House official said on Friday, reversing a cancellation announced only a day earlier. The official said Trump will hold back-to-back rallies in the two states on Sunday, on top of nearly 20 telephone rallies.

On Thursday the Republican National Committee had rolled out a 72-hour sprint of tele-rallies in nearly 20 states instead of the in-person events, and Trump told reporters he did not feel he had to go to Kansas, saying Republican Sen. Roger Marshall was doing very well there. The official said Friday that the in-person rallies were rearranged to fit around the newly added tele-rallies.

The flip-flop drew attention because both races look closer than Republicans expected. Polling averages show Democrat Adam Hamilton slightly ahead of Marshall in Kansas, and the Iowa Senate race, where Rep. Ashley Hinson is the Republican nominee, in a dead heat. Trump has headlined 25 rallies in October and was campaigning in Florida on Friday.

Trump cast his own ballot last weekend in Florida, and more events may be added on Monday before he spends Election Day at the White House.

items.title: Alaska's Senate race turns chaotic: Peltola denies a spoiler plot as the Justice Department expands its probe
items.summary:
Democrat Mary Peltola denied on Thursday that her campaign had anything to do with another candidate named Sullivan appearing on Alaska's Senate ballot. She said she knew nothing about any candidate other than herself and the incumbent, Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, and that she is not interested in tricking voters.

The dispute centres on retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan Jr., one of four finalists for the seat, whom the New York Times reported Peltola campaign staffers helped recruit as a spoiler — a claim her campaign and Senate Democrats' campaign arm deny, and which the other Sullivan also denies. On Thursday the Justice Department expanded a criminal investigation with dozens of new grand jury subpoenas, House Oversight Chairman James Comer opened a House probe, and Trump again called for Peltola to be prosecuted.

Alaska's Supreme Court has ruled both Sullivans can stay on the ballot. Governor Mike Dunleavy has ordered a state investigation, and Trump last week directed the Justice Department to sue to delay results if the incumbent narrowly loses. More than $130 million has poured into the race, a record for a state of about 740,000 people.

Under ranked-choice voting, Alaska will not tally final results before November 18, so the winner — and possibly control of the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53 to 47 edge — may not be known for weeks. About 41,000 Alaskans had already voted by Thursday.

items.title: Justice Department subpoenas California election workers in its noncitizen-voter investigation
items.summary:
Los Angeles County's registrar confirmed on Thursday that election employees have received federal grand jury subpoenas in a criminal investigation into California's voter rolls. At least two employees were served last week and told to appear in court on November 4, the day after the election.

The subpoenas seek testimony and internal records about federal requests for information on alleged noncitizen voting, which the administration says involves thousands of registrations. Earlier this month the Justice Department warned it could prosecute workers who knowingly count noncitizen ballots, in letters sent to 57 of California's 58 counties. A department spokesperson declined to comment on the subpoenas.

The escalation follows a federal judge's ruling on Wednesday rejecting the department's emergency request to set aside about 20,000 ballots from people flagged as likely noncitizens. The judge found no legal basis for the move and said he was not convinced the list was reliable; the department is appealing.

Los Angeles County Registrar Dean Logan said local officials are following state and federal law and called the federal approach confrontational at every step. Reuters has reported more than 100 subpoenas seeking records on tens of thousands of voters in at least 13 states, at least 49 of them under grand jury authority.

items.title: More than 43 million Americans have already voted, at a pace far ahead of past midterms
items.summary:
More than 43 million ballots had been cast by late Thursday in this year's midterms, according to the University of Florida Election Lab — more than a third of everyone who voted in the entire 2022 midterm election, with Election Day still to come on Tuesday. Ballots are arriving at four to five million a day.

Texas is leading the surge, with more than 5.8 million ballots in, about 1.75 million more than its entire 2022 early total. In the roughly half of states that record party registration, Democrats account for about 44 percent of early ballots, Republicans 31.2 percent and unaffiliated voters 24.7 percent. Minneapolis has already set an early-voting record for a non-presidential year.

Election Lab director Michael McDonald cautions that early numbers cannot predict winners: they show who has voted, not how, and Election Day turnout usually tilts more Republican. Overall turnout is on track to rival or pass 2018, the strongest midterm showing in a century.

Early voting is now winding down state by state as Tuesday approaches, shifting the contest to getting remaining supporters to the polls on the day itself.

items.title: Pope Leo becomes the first pontiff ever to cast a ballot in a U.S. election
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV has voted by mail in the U.S. midterms, the Vatican said on Friday — the first time a pope has ever cast a ballot in an American election. The Vatican said he submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago and believes in the right and duty of citizens to take part in democratic processes. It did not say whom he voted for.

Leo, 71, was born in Chicago and is the first American-born pope. He registered in Illinois under his birth name, Robert Francis Prevost, and requested his ballot on October 3, according to the Will County Clerk's office as reported by the Chicago Sun-Times. Illinois voters are choosing a successor to retiring Sen. Dick Durbin and deciding whether to re-elect Gov. JB Pritzker.

The ballot lands against a tense backdrop between the Vatican and the White House. Trump has called Leo weak and terrible on crime; Leo has called threats against Iran's civilisation unacceptable, declined to join Trump's Board of Peace for Gaza, and urged reflection on how migrants are treated in the United States.

Leo was elected in May 2025 to lead the world's 1.4 billion Catholics. He had part of his right lung removed on October 13 after a cancer diagnosis that doctors say needs no further treatment, and he travels to South America next week.

items.title: If Tuesday's results are contested, Congress itself has the final say on who gets seated
items.summary:
Some of Tuesday's closest races may take weeks of recounts and court fights to settle, but the last word belongs to Congress itself. The Constitution makes each chamber the judge of the elections, returns and qualifications of its own members, a Reuters explainer noted on Friday.

House challenges run through the Federal Contested Election Act to the House Administration Committee, which can recommend who should be seated. Senate challenges go to the Senate Rules Committee, though floor fights, filibusters and even boycotts aimed at denying a quorum are possible. Any House fight still open when the new Congress meets in January is decided by the new House, not the old one.

History shows how long this can drag: Minnesota's contested Senate seat stayed empty until July 2009, and a New Hampshire seat in the 1970s was declared vacant and filled only by a special election months later. The House has handled 634 contested elections since 1789.

The stakes are unusually high because both chambers are close — Democrats need a net gain of four seats in each to flip control — and election litigation has hit record levels, with 756 cases counted in the last cycle. Eighteen House races are rated toss-ups, along with as many as seven Senate races.

items.title: Tech sell-off deepens at midday as AI-spending worries hammer stocks
items.summary:
The technology sell-off intensified on Friday, with the Nasdaq Composite down more than 2.5 percent by midday, the S&P 500 off about 1.6 percent and the Dow down roughly 0.7 percent. Results from Amazon and Intel compounded worries that enormous spending on artificial intelligence is not paying back fast enough.

Semiconductor stocks led the fall, and money rotated into defensive corners of the market such as consumer staples and health care. Smaller stocks were hit too, with the Russell 2000 down about 1.75 percent in one midday reading, while oil rose on the fighting around the Strait of Hormuz and Russian refineries.

The rout caps a rough month for the AI trade. The Nasdaq is heading for an October decline of nearly 5 percent, the S&P 500 is slightly down for the month, and the Dow is still on course for a gain of more than 2 percent — a sign investors are not leaving stocks, but are leaving expensive growth names.

Watch the close on Friday and whether buyers step in on Monday, the last trading day before Tuesday's midterms, with more big earnings still ahead.

items.title: Intel plunges about 28 percent in what could be its worst day ever
items.summary:
Intel shares fell about 28 percent on Friday, on track for their largest one-day percentage drop on record, after the chipmaker's fourth-quarter forecast missed badly and a factory accident in Israel shut production for weeks. More than $120 billion in market value was wiped out.

Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, well below the roughly $17 billion analysts expected, and warned the personal computer market will shrink about 12 percent this year and 10 percent next. It blamed a memory-chip shortage: demand from AI data centres is pushing memory and computer prices beyond what PC buyers can stomach.

Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan called the Israel factory accident unfortunate and tragic; Reuters estimated the multiweek shutdown will cost about $600 million in revenue over two quarters. Intel also faces substrate supply bottlenecks, expects no positive cash flow in 2026, and is targeting $20 billion in capital spending.

The damage spread across chips, with AMD down about 9.5 percent, Broadcom about 5 percent and Nvidia roughly 3 percent. Intel's own quarter was not all bleak — third-quarter revenue rose 21 percent and data-centre and AI revenue jumped 78 percent — but investors focused squarely on the outlook.

items.title: Exxon and Chevron profits more than double as war keeps oil prices high
items.summary:
ExxonMobil and Chevron reported third-quarter profits that more than doubled on Friday, powered by oil prices kept high by the U.S.–Iran war and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. Exxon earned $15.4 billion, up from $7.5 billion a year ago, on revenue of about $113 billion, while Chevron's net income nearly tripled to $9.9 billion on $67.8 billion in revenue — both ahead of expectations.

Refining was the standout. Chevron's refining profit rose more than 300 percent to $4.9 billion as its plants ran at 98 percent of capacity and processed a record of more than a million barrels a day, and Exxon's refining earnings of about $7.2 billion roughly matched what it made producing oil. Free cash flow — $19.1 billion at Exxon and $12 billion at Chevron — was the highest since 2022.

Drivers are paying the other side of that trade. The national average gasoline price in the third quarter was $4.12 a gallon, a record for the quarter and 96 cents higher than a year ago, while diesel averaged about $6.32, up 71 percent.

Both stocks are up about 52 percent this year and rose again on Friday morning. Shell, which reported Thursday, also more than doubled its profit, to about $12 billion.

items.title: Anthropic files to go public at a valuation above $900 billion, in what could be the biggest IPO ever
items.summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has filed to go public at a valuation above $900 billion, in an offering that could raise roughly $90 billion — potentially the largest initial public offering in history. The company reported revenue of $4.8 billion for the first nine months of the year, up 173 percent, and a net loss of $1.5 billion.

The filing says Anthropic expects to reach profitability in 2028 and projects revenue growing from $9 billion this year to more than $130 billion in 2029. About 80 percent of its sales come from business customers, and it sells Claude directly, through resellers and through cloud platforms including Amazon, Microsoft and Google.

The planned listing, expected to use the ticker ANTH, would test investor appetite for AI at a moment when that appetite is wobbling — technology stocks were selling off sharply on Friday over doubts about how quickly AI spending pays back. Anthropic's deal could also open the door for rivals OpenAI and SpaceX, which are also weighing listings.

Earlier this month Anthropic reportedly turned down a merger proposal from OpenAI chairman Bret Taylor, telling staff it would go public on its own. Goldman Sachs is leading the offering, with JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley also involved.

items.title: MediaTek says AI chip demand will keep growing, with its first accelerator set to bring in $2.5 billion
items.summary:
Taiwan chip designer MediaTek struck a confident tone on Friday that cut against the sell-off in U.S. technology stocks. Chief Executive Rick Tsai told the company's earnings call that demand for artificial intelligence chips will continue to grow, in his words, for sure, even if the pace varies.

MediaTek's first AI accelerator chip began shipping last month and is expected to generate $2.5 billion in revenue in the fourth quarter alone. A second accelerator is on track for high-volume production in early 2028. Third-quarter revenue rose 18.3 percent from a year ago to about $5.16 billion, and net income rose 10.8 percent.

The company is deliberately shifting beyond smartphones, its traditional base, to become a significant supplier of custom AI chips to big cloud providers, with TSMC as its manufacturing partner. Nvidia invested $3.5 billion in MediaTek's record overseas convertible bond issue in August, and Alphabet also took part.

MediaTek is Taiwan's second-most valuable listed company, at about $200 billion, and its shares are up 174 percent this year despite a 3.2 percent dip on Friday before the results — a reminder that the AI boom looks very different from Taipei than from a jittery Wall Street.

items.title: Reddit stock sinks as Google's AI answers cut its search traffic
items.summary:
Reddit shares plunged on Friday — down roughly 22 percent before the market opened — even though the company beat expectations for the quarter. The problem was not earnings; it was traffic arriving from Google.

Reddit said search referrals fell by more than a million a week on average in October, and Chief Executive Steve Huffman blamed Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, which answer questions directly instead of sending readers onward. U.S. daily users fell 2 percent from a year ago to 50.7 million, global daily users of 130.3 million missed estimates, and the company warned of a low double-digit percentage drop in users next quarter. Its revenue forecast also came in light.

The underlying business still grew fast: third-quarter revenue rose 53 percent to $895 million, advertising made up 95 percent of it, net income jumped 74 percent to $283 million, and data-licensing revenue rose 35 percent to $48 million.

Reddit's response is to test a mainly logged-in experience in some markets outside the U.S. this quarter. Logged-in and app users generate more than 80 percent of its money, and keeping people signed in would improve ad targeting and help protect Reddit's vast archive of human conversation from being scraped to train AI.

items.title: Halloween weather: a dry treat for the East, rare rain and tricks for the West
items.summary:
Halloween on Saturday is shaping up as a split holiday. High pressure should keep the East dry and seasonably cool for trick-or-treating, with only spotty showers in Florida, while much of the central and western United States deals with rain, storms or snow.

Southern California is in for its first rainy Halloween in 30 to 40 years in many cities — San Diego, Palm Springs and Riverside last saw measurable Halloween rain in 1987 — though most places should get less than an inch. In the Sierra Nevada the precipitation could fall as snow, and a Halloween storm there could bring gusts up to 50 miles an hour and several inches at high elevations.

Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected Saturday evening from South Texas to southern Arkansas, including Houston and New Orleans, and flash flooding is possible in central Arizona. The coldest trick-or-treating will be in Montana, Idaho, Wyoming and the Northwest interior, in the 30s and 40s, while the Midwest looks pleasant in the 50s and 60s.

One timing note for families: Halloween night is the last evening of daylight saving time this year. Clocks fall back early Sunday, the earliest possible date for the change.

items.title: A Pineapple Express aims flood risk at California and a still-saturated Southwest
items.summary:
A low-end Pineapple Express — an atmospheric river drawing moisture from near Hawaii — is sending two rounds of rain into the Southwest and California this Halloween weekend, and forecasters say the bigger danger is where the ground is already soaked. Parts of Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Utah took 2 to 5 inches of rain last week that caused major flash flooding.

The first round runs Friday through western Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, with local flash flooding possible near Lubbock and Midland. Rain then builds in Southern California on Saturday, peaks early Sunday, and spreads as Southwest rain and high mountain snow into Monday.

The greatest concern is the Phoenix metro's north and east sides and the Mogollon Rim, southern Utah's canyon country, western Colorado below the snow line, and recent burn scars, where even modest rain can trigger debris flows. The National Weather Service in Flagstaff warned the Little Colorado and Verde rivers could run high for days and urged slot-canyon hikers to consider cancelling.

Moisture over the Four Corners states is forecast at two to three times the late-October average, near a record for Halloween weekend. Higher peaks in the Rockies and Sierra will see snow and slippery passes Sunday into Monday.

items.title: Christa Pike speaks publicly for the first time since surviving her own execution
items.summary:
Christa Pike, who survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her on September 30, has made her first public comments, in a written statement dictated to her lawyers. She said she is in constant pain in her body, arms, hands and throat, still struggles to speak, and woke alone in a hospital confused after having prepared herself to die.

Pike, 50, received two doses of pentobarbital for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of her classmate Colleen Slemmer. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, she is the only person ever to survive being injected with lethal chemicals in an execution. She spent 10 days in hospital, at one point on a ventilator, before returning to a prison medical ward, where she remains largely isolated.

Her lawyers are fighting any second attempt and on Thursday won until late January to file an updated challenge, with the court citing her medical condition. Governor Bill Lee ordered an investigation into what went wrong and postponed another execution planned this year indefinitely, but said this week he is not inclined to commute her sentence.

The victim's mother, May Martinez, said the state owes her an apology and that the attention on Pike has taken attention away from her daughter.

items.title: OB-GYN group issues its own vaccine schedule for pregnancy for the first time
items.summary:
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists has released its own maternal immunization schedule for 2026 — the first time the group has published an independent framework instead of simply following federal guidance. It recommends four vaccines in pregnancy: flu, Tdap, RSV and COVID-19.

The details matter for timing. Flu vaccine can be given in any trimester, ideally by the end of October; Tdap is preferred early in the 27-to-36-week window; and the RSV vaccine Abrysvo is recommended at 32 through 36 weeks during the September 1 to March 1 season in most of the continental U.S., a window extended from the previous end of January. The schedule was endorsed by 13 other medical societies.

The break with Washington is sharpest on COVID-19. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced in May that COVID vaccines are no longer recommended for healthy pregnant women, while the OB-GYN group still recommends them. The group withdrew earlier this year from the CDC's vaccine advisory committee after changes there, and its schedule lines up with the CDC's earlier recommendations.

Leaders of the group said they acted to give clear, evidence-based guidance amid growing misinformation and patient confusion — a nurse-midwifery leader quoted in the announcement put it bluntly: vaccine hesitancy is huge in this country right now.

items.title: SNAP soda and candy bans start November 1 in four more states, with Ohio on the 2027 list
items.summary:
Starting Sunday, November 1, people using SNAP benefits in Montana, North Dakota, South Carolina and Virginia will no longer be able to buy most soda, energy drinks and candy with their benefit cards, under state waivers approved by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The amount of benefits does not change — only what the card can pay for.

Restricted items have to be paid for another way or put back, while staples such as fruit, vegetables, milk, bread and meat remain covered. Each state writes its own restricted list, so a drink blocked in one state may still be allowed in another, and state SNAP agencies are the authoritative source for what counts.

Eight states already have similar limits, including Indiana, Texas, Florida and Arkansas. More are scheduled to follow — Wyoming, Kansas, Missouri, Ohio and Hawaii in 2027 and Nevada in 2028 — while plans in several other states are on hold after a federal judge ruled against the programme in June.

The change lands alongside the annual cost-of-living increase, which raised the maximum benefit on October 1 to $306 a month for one person and $1,023 for a household of four in the continental U.S.

items.title: Cleveland Glenville kicked out of the state football playoffs over Ginn Academy assignments
items.summary:
The Ohio High School Athletic Association has removed Cleveland Glenville from the 2026 football playoffs while it investigates how the Cleveland school district assigned student participation opportunities. Glenville, one of Ohio's most successful programmes, will not play a postseason game this year.

The issue involves Ginn Academy, a magnet school with no sports of its own, run by the district and founded by Glenville coach Ted Ginn Sr. Its students may play sports only at the district school closest to where they live. The association's executive director, Doug Ute, said an audit found many players on Glenville's team should have been playing at other schools this season, and investigators are still looking at the full scope and earlier seasons.

Glenville was the No. 5 seed in Division III, Region 9. Its first-round opponent, No. 12 Hunting Valley University School, now advances automatically and will play No. 4 Salem on Friday, November 6. Glenville won state titles in 2022, 2023 and 2025.

This has happened before: Glenville was removed from the 2018 playoffs for the same infraction, fined $5,000 and placed on probation through 2021. The association gave no timetable for finishing the investigation or deciding on further penalties.

items.title: Morton Salt's Fairport Harbor mine floods, laying off 77 workers and raising road-salt worries
items.summary:
Morton Salt is laying off 77 workers at its Fairport Harbor mine, northeast of Cleveland, after a significant inflow of water was discovered in the mine on October 22. The company filed the required WARN notice with the state, covering 69 hourly union employees and eight salaried workers, with layoffs dated October 26 and no bumping rights.

The timing is what worries local road crews. The Fairport Harbor mine supplies road salt for winter, and several Northeast Ohio counties contract with it. Portage County's engineer says the county has 3,000 to 3,500 tons on hand but typically uses 4,000 to 4,500 tons in a winter to cover about 736 lane miles.

Ashtabula, Geauga, Lake, Mahoning and Trumbull counties also rely on the mine for salt, according to Cleveland.com reporting. Whether an actual shortage develops depends on how long the mine stays closed and how harsh the winter turns out to be.

Officials say the situation is being monitored. For now, counties head into the season with thinner stockpiles than planned and a key supplier sidelined.

items.title: Ohio measles cases surge to 296, nearly six times last year's total, in the state's third outbreak of 2026
items.summary:
Ohio recorded 36 new measles cases in the past week — up from eight the week before — bringing the state's 2026 total to 296 cases across 24 counties, according to the Ohio Department of Health. That is 557 percent more than the 45 cases Ohio saw in all of 2025.

Pike County reported 20 of the new cases in what is now Ohio's third measles outbreak of the year. In Northeast Ohio, Geauga County has the state's highest listed count at 54, followed by Ashtabula at 47, Wayne at 45 and Medina at 27, while Cuyahoga County has three. Akron Children's Hospital also announced a possible exposure at its main hospital building on October 20.

Health officials say the vast majority of Ohio cases are in unvaccinated people, and state health director Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff urged Ohioans to be fully vaccinated. Ohio's MMR coverage for children and adolescents was 91.5 percent in 2023, below the level above 95 percent generally needed for herd immunity.

Nationally, Johns Hopkins data put the U.S. total at 4,730 cases so far in 2026 — the highest annual count since 1991 and already more than double last year's total.

items.title: Cost of living tops Ohio voters' concerns days before the midterms, a new survey finds
items.summary:
Asked what concerns them most heading into Tuesday's midterms, Ohio voters put the cost of living first by a wide margin. In a survey of 1,200 registered Ohio voters, 66 percent named cost of living, followed by health care at 44 percent, affordable housing at 31 percent and data centres at 22 percent.

The numbers behind the worry are concrete. Prices for gasoline rose 34.2 percent in the year to September and fuel oil 74.2 percent, while the average Ohio gas price stood at $4.22 a gallon on October 30. About 161,000 Ohioans dropped Affordable Care Act marketplace coverage between February 2025 and February 2026 — a 32.4 percent decline, the largest percentage drop in the nation — after enhanced federal subsidies were not renewed.

Data centres making the top four reflects Ohio's position: the state ranks fifth nationally, state tax breaks for the industry are estimated at $141.8 million, and local fights over electricity and water use have led places such as Nelsonville to ban them and Athens to pass a one-year moratorium.

The survey, conducted in late September by Better Choices for Democracy, Centerline Research and Harris Poll, suggests affordability — especially fuel and health care — is the lens most Ohio voters will carry into the booth on November 3.

items.title: Cook Political Report moves 12 more House races toward Democrats, including Ohio's 9th
items.summary:
The Cook Political Report shifted 12 more U.S. House races toward Democrats on Friday, eight of them seats currently held by Republicans — its second move in a week, after shifting 19 races the same direction on October 23. The changes, days before Tuesday's election, reflect a late map tilting toward Democrats.

Ohio's 9th District, represented by Democrat Marcy Kaptur, moved from Toss Up to Lean Democratic — notable because the district was redrawn in October 2025 to be significantly more Republican. Kaptur, seeking a 23rd term against Republican Derek Merrin, led 49 percent to 43 percent in a recent poll cited in Friday coverage. A separate Ohio move took the 1st District from Lean Democratic to Likely Democratic.

Other Friday shifts included Republican-held seats in Pennsylvania and Indiana moving from Likely Republican to Lean Republican. Analysts cited in the coverage project Democrats could reach as many as 240 House seats if they flip between 12 and 25 seats.

Ratings are not results, and redrawn districts make history a weaker guide than usual. But two consecutive weekly shifts in the same direction is the kind of late signal campaigns watch when deciding where to spend their final dollars.

items.title: Olivia Rodrigo wears an 'Amy Acton for Governor' shirt on stage in Columbus
items.summary:
Pop star Olivia Rodrigo closed her Columbus concert on Thursday night wearing a white T-shirt that read 'Amy Acton for Governor,' keeping it on for her final three songs at the Schottenstein Center on Ohio State's campus. She urged the crowd to vote in Tuesday's midterms.

Rodrigo told the audience she had filled out her own absentee ballot earlier that Thursday and spent the day exploring Columbus, according to Columbus Dispatch reporting. Acton, the Democratic nominee, reposted a photo of Rodrigo in the shirt with the caption 'Ohio loves you.'

Acton, a physician and Ohio's former state health director, faces Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Libertarian Don Kissick on November 3, in one of the most closely watched governor's races in the country. Celebrity endorsements rarely move statewide races on their own, but they do generate the kind of social-media reach campaigns cannot easily buy in the final weekend.

The moment also landed in the middle of a heated final stretch in the race, including a controversy over a Ramaswamy campaign ad involving Acton's estranged mother, whose planned run the Ramaswamy campaign has since confirmed has ended.

baby.tip: Dress-rehearse the hospital run: drive the route once together, note where to park and where to check in after hours, and keep the car topped up with fuel. With the car-seat base already installed, one calm practice trip now means the real one is just a drive, not a scramble.
baby.fact: A newborn's stomach is tiny at first — about the size of a cherry on day one and a walnut by day three — which is exactly why little-and-often feeds are the plan at the start. That small capacity grows fast over the first month.
